rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of al-Nābigha’s poem is exceptionally beautiful and eloquently conveys distress and a long, sleepless night; it was said no poet began better.
rows.anchor: متناه في الحسن , بليغ في وصف ما شكاه , من همه وطول ليله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of a chest relieved by night borrows from a shepherd settling camels at their nighttime resting place; its natural ease joins eloquence and sweetness.
rows.anchor: وصدر أراح الليل عزب همه مستعار من إراحة الراعي الإبل إلى مباتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s lines are accomplished, but al-Imruʾ al-Qays surpasses them in crafted technique, simile, and inventive meanings.
rows.anchor: إلا أن في أبيات امرئ القيس من ثقافة الصنعة وحسن التشبيه وإبداع المعاني ما ليس في أبيات النابغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Imruʾ al-Qays gives night a body and compares gathering darkness to successive, colliding sea waves.
rows.anchor: جعل لليل صلبا وأعجازا وكلكلا , وشبه تراكم ظلمة الليل بموج البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He depicts the stars as firmly rope-bound, motionless, and unable to depart, intensifying the night’s oppressive stillness.
rows.anchor: وجعل النجوم كأنها مشدودة بحبال وثيقة فهي راكدة لا تزول ولا تبرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem first longs for dawn as relief, then reverses course: the affliction is too great for any time to end or cure it.
rows.anchor: فزعم أن البلوى أعظم من أن يكون لها في شيء من الأوقات كشف وانجلاء

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: The report says al-Walīd stamped his foot while hearing the poem, and al-Shaʿbī declared the matter settled, signaling recognition of al-Imruʾ al-Qays’s excellence.
rows.anchor: قال فركض الوليد برجله , فقال الشعبي: بانت القضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A comparison of competing poems distinguishes their levels by deciding whether one leads, the other falls short, or they are equal.
rows.anchor: فبمثل هذه الأمور تعتبر معاني المعارضة فيقع بها الفصل بين الكلامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When poets share a subject, one can reach its summit while the other falls short; al-Aʿshā’s treatment of wine outdoes al-Akhṭal’s.
rows.anchor: فيرتقي أحدهما إلى ذروته ويقصر شأو الآخر عن مساواته في درجته , كالأعشى والأخطل

rows.speaker: هشام ابن أدهم المازني
rows.claim: Hishām reports that al-Shaʿbī visited a drunken al-Akhṭal, who boasted of his wine verse; al-Shaʿbī preferred al-Aʿshā’s verse, and al-Akhṭal conceded.
rows.anchor: هشام ابن أدهم المازني -وكان علامة - قال: دخل الشعبي على الأخطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhṭal says the wine’s aroma reaches a person with a cold, whereas al-Aʿshā makes its sharp aroma dispel congestion and cure the ailment, a stronger image.
rows.anchor: وقد طبت لدائه وتأيت لبرئه وشفائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A more striking form of poetic contest builds something up and then demolishes it, or establishes an idea before reversing it.
rows.anchor: بناء الشيء وهدمه , وتشييده ثم وضعه ونقضه

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Jabala asked Ḥassān to disparage wine because it had captivated him; Ḥassān began a verse saying the cup would otherwise be worth nothing to its drinker.
rows.anchor: قال حسان: أتيت جبلة بني الأيهم الغساني وقد مدحته فقال لي: يا أبا الوليد

rows.speaker: ابن الخطاب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s maxim urges restraint in grammatical censure: the most discerning grammarian is one who does not fault anyone’s speech.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الخطاب: أنحى الناس من لم يلحن أحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no contradiction between the forms: the Prophet’s eager critics would have seized on it if they had understood it as a contradiction, but they knew the usage the questioner missed.
rows.anchor: فلو كان هذا عندهم مناقضة لتعلقوا به وأسرعوا بالرد عليه , ولكن القوم علموا وجهلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may insert lā and cancel its negating force; the cited line has lā in a phrase meaning that he traveled in a well without realizing it.
rows.anchor: العرب قد تدخل لا في أثناء كلامها وتلغي معناها , كقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can also leave lā unspoken while its sense is understood; the poet’s wish that the poor man return successful illustrates the omitted particle.
rows.anchor: العرب تذكر لا وتلغيه ولا تضمر لا وتستعمله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One analysis treats the bāʾ in the phrase as extra, leaving the sense that whoever intends wrongdoing there; Arabic can add particles without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: قد قيل إن الباء زائدة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr says the Arabic of the Qurʾān and the Prophet’s contemporaries differed from the language of his own era, explaining why old usages may sound unfamiliar later.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمروا بن العلاء: اللسان الذي نزل به القرآن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An unnamed view holds that Arabic retained its original form and character until the Umayyad period, when corruption altered it.
rows.anchor: وقد زعم بعضهم أن كلام العرب كان باقيا على نجره الأول وعلى سنخ طبعه الأقدم إلى زمان بني أمية

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr recites archaic verses by Imruʾ al-Qays and al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza and laments that the people who understood such diction have disappeared.
rows.anchor: أن أبا عمرو أنشد قول الحارث بن حلزة: زعموا أن كل من ضرب العي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars rely on pre-Islamic, contemporaneous, and next-generation poets, not later poets such as Bashshār, Abū Nuwās, and Dibil, because later Arabic had changed.
rows.anchor: ولهذا صار العلماء لا يحتجون بشعر المحدثين , ولا يستشهدون به كبشار بن برد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will create affection for them in believers’ hearts; the phrase does not mean that God loved someone in the ordinary human sense.
rows.anchor: إنما المعنى أن الله سيجعل لهم في قلوب المؤمنين , أي يخلق لهم في صدور المؤمنين مودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The use of jaʿala as ‘create’ is supported by the parallel statement that God made spouses from people’s own kind, meaning created them.
rows.anchor: كقوله عز وجل: {والله جعل لكم من أنفسكم أزواجا} أي خلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both radiftuhu and radiftu lahu are eloquent Arabic forms, like naṣaḥtuhu and naṣaḥtu lahu.
rows.anchor: فإنهم لغتان فصيحتان: ردفته وردفت له كما تقول: نصحته ونصحت له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in this Qurʾānic construction belongs to older Arabic usage, though it became rare among later speakers.
rows.anchor: ودخول الباء فيه فإن هذا الحرف كثيرا ما يوجد في كلام العرب الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān explains its repeated stories and reports as a way for people to remember and take heed, citing its statements that the message was repeatedly conveyed and warnings varied.
rows.anchor: وقد أخبر الله عز وجل بالسبب الذي من أجله كرر الأقاصيص والأخبار في القرآن فقال سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Raḥmān addresses humans and jinn, recounts diverse blessings, and renews the refrain after each section to elicit acknowledgement and gratitude.
rows.anchor: وأما سورة الرحمن فإن الله سبحانه خاطب بها الثقلين من الإنس والجن , وعدد عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Mursalāt repeatedly renews warnings as it recounts each condition of the Last Day, strengthening the proof and leaving no excuse.
rows.anchor: ذكر أحوال يوم القيامة وأهوالها فقدم الوعيد فيها وجدد القول عند ذكر كل حال من أحوالها

words: يرسل عليكما شواظ من نار ونحاس فلا تنتصران
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A warning that guards people from punishment is itself a blessing, parallel to promised reward; one recognizes a thing by considering its opposite.
rows.anchor: إن نعمة الله تعالى فيما أنذر به وحذر من عقوباته على معاصيه ليحذروها

rows.speaker: بعض حكماء الشعراء
rows.claim: An unnamed wise poet says hardship teaches a person what bliss is, supporting the use of opposites to clarify blessings and warnings.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا ما قاله بعض حكماء الشعراء:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Critics argue that separating Qurʾānic stories, admonitions, parables, and rulings into different sūras would improve arrangement, memorability, and clarity.
rows.anchor: وأما قولهم: لو كان نزول القرآن على سبيل التفصيل والتقسيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining varied meanings in one sūra or short verse yields broader benefit: a disbelieving listener encounters proof across many subjects, while separated topics would prove only one.
rows.anchor: اجتماع المعاني الكثيرة في السورة الواحدة أوفر حظا وأجدى نفعا من التمييز والتفريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase has an ellipsis: understand the warning as punishment or torment, as was sent down on those who split the Qurʾān into parts.
rows.anchor: فإن فيه محذوفا يدل ظاهر الكلام عليه؛ كأنه قال: أنا النذير المبين عقوبة أو عذابا

words: كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intervening description of faith does not break the syntax: it elaborates a matter with many parts, then the passage returns to compare aversion to the spoils with aversion to departure.
rows.anchor: ثم عطف بالكلام على أول الفصل فقال: {كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق وإن فريقا من المؤمنين لكارهون}

words: لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to the Prophet is a necessary aside prompted by the moment; like asking a distracted listener to attend, it resumes rather than breaks the surrounding discourse.
rows.anchor: قيل هذا عارض من حال دعت الحاجة إلى ذكره , فلم يجز تركه ولا تأخيره عن وقته

words: لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the unlettered Prophet moved his tongue to memorize fresh revelation, he was told to understand it and leave its collection and preservation to God.
rows.anchor: وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أميا لا يقرأ ولا يكتب

words: لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet moved his tongue while receiving revelation because he feared it would slip away from him.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله سبحانه: {لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به} قال: كان يحرك به لسانه مخافة أن يتفلت منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eloquence does not require obscure vocabulary: the Qurʾān’s balanced register combines grandeur with sweetness and ease, while many rare long words are harsh and shunned by rhetoricians.
rows.anchor: فليست الغرابة مما شرطناه في حدود البلاغة , وإنما يكثر وحشي الغريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says that ‘the wolf ate him’ is weak diction because predators are more properly said to tear prey apart.
rows.anchor: كقوله: {فأكله الذئب} وإنما يستعمل مثل هذا في فعل السباع خصوصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection asks how a measure can be called easy or difficult, except when the quantity itself is small.
rows.anchor: قالوا: وما اليسير والعسير من الكيل والاكتيال , وما وجه اختصاصه بهذه

words: وانطلق الملأ منهم أن امشوا واصبروا على آلهتكم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says ‘walk’ is not the strongest expression here and that ‘proceed’ or ‘go forth’ would sound better.
rows.anchor: والمشي في هذا ليس بأبلغ الكلام , ولو قيل بدل ذلك أن امضوا وانطلقوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says halāk is used for concrete people and things, not abstractions such as authority or knowledge.
rows.anchor: وكقوله: {هلك عني سلطانيه} وإنما يستعمل لفظ الهلاك في الأعيان والأشخاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection calls the construction awkward, since speakers would say that they are intense in their love of someone or wealth.
rows.anchor: وأنت لا تسمع فصيحا يقول: أنا لحب زيد شديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says that Arabic does not say someone ‘does zakāh’; it uses verbs such as give, pay, or purify one’s wealth.
rows.anchor: ولا يقول أحد من الناس: فعل زيد الزكاة , إنما يقال: زكى الرجل ماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection questions whether anyone would use jaʿala with wudd to mean that he made someone beloved or loved someone.
rows.anchor: إن الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات سيجعل لهم الرحمن ودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān’s coordination of diverse elements into a coherent whole exceeds human capacity, leaving people unable to produce a comparable work or counter-form.
rows.anchor: ومعلوم أن الإتيان بمثل هذه الأمور , والجمع بين شتاتها حتى تنتظم وتتسق أمر تعجز عنه قوى البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents alternately called the Qurʾān poetry because it is ordered and sorcery because they could not match it; its sweetness and effect on hearts unsettled them.
rows.anchor: يقولون مرة إنه شعر لما رأوه كلاما منظوما , ومرة سحر إذ رأوه معجوزا عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author tentatively identifies the man who deliberated over the Qurʾān as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra; the Qurʾān recounts his reflection and his claim that it was human speech and sorcery.
rows.anchor: ويقال هو الوليد بن المغيرة المخزومي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The central principle of eloquence is placing each kind of word in its most fitting position; substitution either corrupts meaning or removes stylistic brilliance.
rows.anchor: عمود هذه البلاغة التي تجمع لها هذه الصفات هو وضع كل نوع من الألفاظ التي تشتمل عليها فصول الكلام موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Words often mistaken for synonyms—such as knowledge and recognition, praise and gratitude, or stinginess and miserliness—retain distinguishing nuances despite partial overlap.
rows.anchor: لأن كل لفظة منها خاصية تتميز بها عن صاحبتها في بعض معانيها وإن كانا قد يشتركان في بعضها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿrifa takes one object, as in knowing Zayd, whereas ʿilm takes two, as in knowing Zayd to be intelligent.
rows.anchor: وعلمت يقتضي مفعولين , كقولك: علمت زيدا عاقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says one says ‘I recognize God’ but not ‘I know God’ without an accompanying attribute, such as knowing Him to be just or powerful.
rows.anchor: فتقول عرفت الله , ولا تقول علمت الله , إلا أن تضيف إليه صفة من الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fragment cites an Arabic idiom in which a man ‘walks’ when he has many children; the line about a sheep not walking on the wolf means it does not reproduce abundantly.
rows.anchor: مشى الرجل إذا كثر ولده. وأنشدوا:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphor can be stronger than literal wording: ‘strip’ for the night’s removal of day and ‘proclaim’ for openly carrying out a command are more forceful than literal alternatives.
rows.anchor: والسلخ ها هنا مستعار وهو أبلغ منه لو قال نخرج من النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling authority destroyed is stronger than saying it went away, since something that merely departs may return, while destruction leaves no remnant or reversal.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن الذهاب قد يكون على مراصدة العود , وليس مع الهلاك بقيا ولا رجعى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation takes sulṭāniya here to mean proof and argument.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن معنى السلطان ها هنا الحجة والبرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shadīd here means miserly; Arabic also calls a miser shadīd or mutashaddid, as illustrated by Ṭarafa’s verse.
rows.anchor: وأن الشديد معناه هاهنا البخيل , ويقال: رجل شديد ومتشدد أي بخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām means ‘because of love of wealth’; khayr denotes wealth, and the phrase describes miserliness driven by that love.
rows.anchor: واللام في قوله: {لحب الخير} بمعنى لأجل حب الخير وهو المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Doers of zakāh’ conveys sustained, habitual performance as a defining trait, whereas ordinary verbs merely report that payment occurred; this is the most complete and forceful wording.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الكلام ومراده المبالغة في أدائها والمواظبة عليه حتى يكون ذلك صفة لازمة لهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes zakāh here as righteous work and virtuous deeds, so the phrase means that they perform good and pure actions.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن معنى الزكاة هنا العمل الصالح الزاكي

rows.speaker: المعترضون
rows.claim: Critics propose arranging sūras by subject—stories together, admonitions and parables together, and rulings elsewhere—for better organization, memorization, and clarity.
rows.anchor: قالوا: لو كانت سور القرآن على هذا الترتيب فتكون أخبار الأمم وأقاصيصهم في سورة , والمواعظ والأمثال في سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iftirās by a predator means killing, while the brothers claimed the wolf consumed Joseph entirely; ‘ate’ therefore accurately conveys their claim that no trace remained.
rows.anchor: فأما قوله تعالى: {فأكله الذئب} فإن الافتراس معناه في فعل السبع القتل فحسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers said the wolf ate him to forestall their father’s demand for surviving evidence that could prove their story false.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنهم خافوا مطالبة أبيهم إياه بأثر باق منه يشهد بصحة ما ذكروه

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkīt records the idiom ‘the wolf ate the sheep and left no trace of it,’ supporting the Qurʾānic wording.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن السكيت في ألفاظ العرب قولهم: أكل الذئب الشاة فما ترك منها تامورا

rows.speaker: بعض شعرائهم
rows.claim: An anonymous poet calls a wolf an eater when it sees blood on its companion, using eating for a predator’s attack.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض شعرائهم: فتى ليس لابن العم كالذئب إن رأى

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: Another poet says his people were not eaten by a hyena, further attesting to broad Arabic use of ‘eat’ for a beast’s attack.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: أبا خراشة أما أنت ذا نفر

rows.speaker: عتبة بن أبي لهب
rows.claim: In the report, after the Prophet prayed for a dog to be sent against ʿUtba, a lion attacked him; he cried that the beast was eating him.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عتبة بن أبي لهب أنه لما دعا عليه السلام: فقال اللهم سلط عليه كلبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic extends ‘eat’ to bites, stings, and pinches; a report about a scorpion near a small child illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: وقد يتوسع في ذلك حتى يجعل العقر أكلا وكذلك اللدغ واللسع
